Customs Service Press Release
Shows How Increased Enforcement of Prohibition Encourages Hard Drug Use

The following cliché filled press release boasts about increased seizures. Great going, but look at what they seized.

The largest percentage increase, by far, was marijuana, 47%
versus only a 32% increase in cocaine and just a 13% increase in heroin seized.

But now look at the absolute amounts:
548,262 pounds of marijuana, 72,535 pounds of cocaine, and 1,280 pounds of heroin.

Usually, the largest percentage increases are easiest for the lowest absolute amounts. Not here.

Marijuana seizures are over 7 times the volume of cocaine and over 400 times the volume of heroin!

It isn’t that they are ignoring the hard drugs. The fact is that marijuana is much bulkier than the hard drugs, and so when there is an increase in enforcement, there will be relatively more marijuana found than hard drugs, which are much easier to hide.

This means so long as marijuana remains contraband for the Customs Service to seize, whenever there is an increase in enforcement, the supply of marijuana will go down more than the supply of hard drugs. This report is just more evidence of that.

The fact is that every time there has been an increase in enforcement efforts, there has been a hard drug epidemic. Last time it was crack. This time it is heroin and speed.
See How the Narcs Created Crack

Of course, as this puffery illustrates, there are good bureaucratic reasons for concentrating on marijuana. The numbers are impressive. The objective of this release is to get an increase in funding for Customs from conservative Republicans who are heavily into reefer madness.)

WASHINGTON, Aug. 17, 1998 /PRNewswire/ --

The U.S. Customs Service today announced that final results from Operation Brass Ring, a six-month-long nationwide intensified enforcement effort to increase drug seizures, show that Customs grabbed significantly more drugs while reaching for the Brass Ring: total amounts of cocaine, marijuana and heroin seized from February 1 to July 31, 1998 have increased by 45 percent over the same time period as last year.

These figures show that the amount of marijuana seized is up 47 percent

Seizures of currency are up 45 percent, while controlled deliveries skyrocketed by a whopping 100 percent during the same time period, resulting in an 82 percent increase in arrests as a result of controlled deliveries.

"These outstanding results reaffirm that the workforce of the U.S. Customs Service remains single-mindedly dedicated to its mission of protecting our country by seizing this poison before it can get to our streets, our schools and our children," said Raymond W. Kelly, Commissioner of the U.S. Customs Service.

"Customs reached for that Brass Ring and we struck gold. Drug and currency seizures are up dramatically, Customs employees are energized and revitalized, and the lessons we learned in creativity and innovation will help us keep our momentum going."

During the 180-day period of Operation Brass Ring, final figures show that Customs seized 548,262 pounds of marijuana, 72,535 pounds of cocaine, and 1,280 pounds of heroin. Customs also seized $43.7 million in undeclared currency. There were 220 controlled deliveries, resulting in 414 arrests.

Operation Brass Ring also helped Customs dramatically increase overall volume of seizures of all narcotics: as of June 30, one month before the end of Operation Brass Ring, Customs had seized more than one million pounds of narcotics (cocaine, heroin, marijuana, methamphetamine, opium and other illegal narcotics) during Fiscal Year (FY) 1998 to date, more than Customs had seized during all of FY-1997. Customs seizes more illegal drugs than all other federal agencies combined.

"But it doesn’t stop here," continued Commissioner Kelly, "you can be sure of that. The spirit of creativity and innovation that Operation Brass Ring engendered in the ranks of Customs employees gives us great momentum. The tremendous wealth of experience and ingenuity in Customs has been tapped, and we are just beginning to learn what the field can do when empowered locally."

Operation Brass Ring was a 180-day enforcement effort intended to dramatically increase drug seizures at high-risk ports of entry. The enforcement action focused on the use of innovative, unpredictable and random enforcement operations at air, sea and land border ports of entry through a multi-faceted partnership effort that included inspectors, special agents, and union representatives. Unique in Customs enforcement history, Operation Brass Ring was field-based and field-driven, with emphasis on local solutions to local problems and sharing of best practices nationwide. Although 42 high- risk ports were initially identified as required to participate in Operation Brass Ring, ultimately 129 ports of entry submitted and carried out action plans as part of this historic operation.

Operation Brass Ring success stories are as many and as varied as there are different ports of entry and Customs employees:

Two suspects in the murder of a mentally handicapped young girl were apprehended at the Eagle Pass port of entry while attempting to leave the United States;

A husband and wife in their 70s were arrested in Blaine, Washington while attempting to smuggle in 24 lbs of marijuana in the trunk of their car; (Ed. note: A major victory! How strange that they would brag about this.)

More than $1.5 million in cash concealed in board games destined for Bogota, Colombia was seized at Houston’s Bush Intercontinental Airport during an outbound Operation Brass Ring enforcement action;

One ton of marijuana was seized in Chicago from a railroad flat car arriving in-bond from Mexico, and six people were arrested;

4,300 pounds of cocaine with a street value of nearly $200 million was seized from a cooking grease tanker in Laredo, Texas;

In the largest cocaine seizure in South Carolina’s history, a joint law enforcement team snagged more than 3,000 pounds of cocaine and arrested a number of dockworkers at the port of Charleston, South Carolina;

More than 3,000 pounds of marijuana was seized in Lukeville, Arizona over a two-week period in April/May during intensified Operation Brass Ring inspections;

More than 4,000 pounds of cocaine was seized from a private yacht in Ft. Lauderdale, Florida, the largest seizure from a private vessel in South Florida’s history;

Customs agents in Newark, assisted by DEA and the New Jersey National Guard, arrested four people and seized 1,300 lbs of cocaine in industrial-sized paper rolls;

Near Pittsburg, New Hampshire, Customs, in two joint operations with the Border Patrol and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) seized 862 full-grown marijuana plants (over 450 pounds of marijuana). (Ed. note: This means that the mature plants weighed only half a pound each. This is inconsistent with the usual claims that the plants yield over a pound of marijuana each. Legally they may count as a kilo each for sentencing purposes in DEAland.)

The "out of the box" thinking and creative "enforcement laboratory" environment fostered by Operation Brass Ring led to many cooperative efforts and exchanges among disciplines and ports within Customs, between Customs and other federal, state and local law enforcement entities; and with Customs’ colleagues in foreign law enforcement agencies such as the RCMP.

Strike teams composed of inspectors and agents from different ports traveled to other ports to share and learn best practices. Interdisciplinary teams used off-the-shelf technology to improve work processes and fined contraband. Many ports made changes in the FIS (federal inspection services) areas, including changing traffic patterns and closely monitoring use of communications devices by people waiting to enter the United States.

Customs has learned many valuable lessons from Operation Brass Ring, and information gathered from this law enforcement effort will take some time to analyze. From valuable intelligence about the way smugglers operate, to patterns of trafficking and displacement, to the fresh perspectives and new ways of doing business generated by six months of brainstorming, Operation Brass Ring will continue to improve Customs performance long after the "official" end of the initiative. Customs will hold a post-Brass Ring Conference in October to discuss these results and plan the agency’s next steps.
